02 Case study · SkyCrypt · Since May 2026

Intelligence behind
autonomous flight.

SkyCrypt treats the drone as a platform and intelligence as the product: one modular AI layer for perception, reasoning, autonomy, collaboration, prediction, and human-supervised control — designed to serve multiple aerial missions on two airframe classes.

Role

ChallengeHow it worksArchitecturePlatformsOutcomesGallery
01

Challenge

Automation follows instructions. Intelligence interprets a mission.

Most drone software is tied to one airframe and one task. SkyCrypt asks how a single intelligence layer can serve many aerial missions while keeping the operator in charge, enforcing explicit safety boundaries, and recording every decision for review.

02

My contribution

From mission concept to working AI Core.

I lead SkyCrypt end to end: I defined the mission concept and the six-capability architecture, specified the dual-platform 5-inch / 10-inch reference design, and drove the AI Core v0.2 prototype — the perception pipeline, event rules, mission assistant, dashboard, and its backend test suite.

  • Product vision, capability model, and brand system
  • Technical dossier for the dual-platform design
  • AI Core v0.2: perception, rules, assistant, dashboard, tests

How it works

Two loops. One operator in charge.

The perception loop turns video into evidence. The mission loop turns a request into a validated configuration — but only the operator can apply it.

  1. CaptureWebcam stream or uploaded video
  2. DetectYOLO11 nano inference with confidence scores
  3. TrackByteTrack assigns persistent track IDs
  4. Apply rulesDeterministic zone-entry events in normalized image zones
  5. RecordSQLite mission history and CSV event export
  6. ReviewStreamlit dashboard for the operator

    Validated outcomes · AI Core v0.2

    What the AI Core delivers.

    Live detection & tracking

    YOLO11 nano inference with ByteTrack tracking on live webcam input and uploaded video.

    Deterministic zone events

    Zone-entry rules over normalized image zones, with every event exportable to CSV.

    Validated mission proposals

    An assistant drafts missions via Ollama (offline) or OpenAI (online); only recognized classes, normalized zones, and bounded thresholds pass validation.

    Mission history

    A Streamlit dashboard backed by SQLite keeps missions, detections, and events reviewable.

    7 / 7

    Backend tests passing

    Rule, validation, and provider-adapter tests run with the standard library and pass.

    Engineering decisions

    Safety before spectacle.

    01Human authority over AI recommendations

    Operator authority supersedes AI-generated recommendations. The assistant proposes mission settings; the operator reviews and applies them. Nothing the model writes changes the system on its own.

    02Explicit input and output contracts

    Mission proposals are limited to recognized classes, normalized image zones, and bounded confidence thresholds. Invalid or reversed bounds are rejected before they reach the pipeline.

    03Provider-independent intelligence

    The same validated contract sits behind an offline Ollama adapter and an online OpenAI adapter, so the assistant works with or without connectivity.

    04Acceptance criteria before field claims

    The dual-platform dossier defines endurance, detection quality, latency, telemetry reliability, and flight safety as explicit acceptance items for each airframe class.

    01

    Problem

    Traditional security is reactive.

    Signature rules struggle with unfamiliar behavior, and concurrent attacks plus alert fatigue slow human-led investigation. The research question: can an AI agent select useful defensive actions at machine speed?

    02

    My contribution

    Lead author across the full research lifecycle.

    I designed and researched the system and led technical research, system design, experimentation, integration, testing, and documentation — from the Markov Decision Process formulation and reward design to the operations platform that surfaces agent decisions to analysts.

    • MDP formulation, state and action design, reward shaping
    • PPO vs DQN comparison under common CybORG conditions
    • Full-stack platform with secure, role-scoped workflows

    Autonomous decision architecture

    Sense → learned policy → act → feedback.

    Step through the closed loop. Each stage hands a concrete artifact to the next; the reward signal closes the loop and drives learning.

          Step 1 of 4

          Controlled CybORG evaluation

          Methodology, objectives & targets.

          1. 01
            Enterprise environment

            10 simulated hosts across 3 subnets (User, Server, DMZ) plus an external attacker network.

          2. 02
            Adversarial testing

            6 attack categories plus 1 concurrent multi-vector test.

          3. 03
            Algorithm comparison

            PPO vs DQN head-to-head in identical CybORG simulation: 500k training steps each, paired t-test on 100 evaluation episodes per scenario.

          4. 04
            Multi-term reward

            Rewards detection, containment, and availability; the false-positive penalty (1.5) exceeds the detection reward (1.0) to prevent an over-aggressive “block everything” policy.

          ≥95%Attack detection
          ≤10 msDecision latency (P99)
          ≤5%False positives
          ≥98%Service uptime

          Objectives and targets from the ACDS research poster, alongside AUC-ROC ≥ 0.95 and convergence within 400k steps.
